items.reply: This is as specified: the spec and the settled grill answer put --shout before the name, and other flag positions are out of scope. Extra arguments after the name were ignored before this change too, so `greet.sh ada --shout` printing `hello ada` is unchanged behaviour.

finding.proof: bin/greet.sh:9 `echo "${line}"`: POSIX leaves echo's backslash handling implementation-defined; on macOS /bin/sh, `sh bin/greet.sh 'a\tb'` now prints a real tab, where the old printf '%s\n' printed `a\tb`.
finding.claim: echo interprets backslash escapes in the name, so output changes even without --shout, breaking the spec's 'without --shout nothing changes'.
finding.suggestion: Print the line with `printf '%s\n' "${line}"` instead of `echo "${line}"`.

items.reply: Fair point, but the spec only asks for capitals and names no non-ASCII case, and POSIX sh has no portable multibyte upcase: GNU tr works byte by byte even with [:lower:]/[:upper:]. We'll leave it for its own change if non-ASCII names come up.

POSIX sh has no boolean type, so a variable holding a value is the usual way to keep a flag. The argument is shifted away on line 5 so the name can be read as $1, which means a later `if` on the argument isn't possible without re-testing it before the shift. Keeping `shout` lets the parse and the upcase stay separate.
Confirmed: with only --shout, the shift leaves $1 unset, name falls back to world, and `sh bin/greet.sh --shout` prints `HELLO WORLD`.

finding.claim: No test covers --shout at all: tests/greet_test.sh only checks `greet.sh ada`, so the bare `--shout` fallback to HELLO WORLD can regress unnoticed.
finding.suggestion: Add to tests/greet_test.sh: `[ "$(sh "$(dirname "$0")/../bin/greet.sh" --shout)" = "HELLO WORLD" ]`, and one for `--shout ada` giving `HELLO ADA`.
